Medicine
MED-i-sin
noun
From the Latin medicina, the healing art or a remedy, from medeor, to heal. It renders the Hebrew gehah, a cure, and teruphah, a healing or remedy — that which is applied to a wound to make it whole.

Biblical Definition

Medicine in Scripture is a remedy applied to a wound, and the Bible speaks of it without the least suspicion. Proverbs makes the boldest use of the word: “A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones” (Pro 17:22). The state of the soul works upon the body as a remedy works upon a sore; gladness in God is medicinal, and settled sorrow wastes the frame. Ezekiel sets medicine at the end of his temple vision, where the river runs out from the sanctuary and the trees upon its banks bear fruit for meat and their leaf for medicine (Eze 47:12) — a picture the Revelation takes up when the leaves of the tree of life are for the healing of the nations. So the ultimate medicine flows from the sanctuary, from God Himself. But the word also stands in the prophets as a warning. Jeremiah says of Egypt, “in vain shalt thou use many medicines; for thou shalt not be cured” (Jer 46:11), and of Zion, “thou hast no healing medicines” (Jer 30:13). Medicines are real, lawful, and often effectual, and they are not almighty. There is a wound they cannot reach, and a nation that piles up remedies while refusing the LORD is heaping up figs against a mortal disease. Balm grows in Gilead; the question Jeremiah asks is why the health of the daughter of his people is not recovered.

Webster 1828 Definition

Any substance administered for the cure of disease; the healing art; whatever serves to remedy or restore.

expand to see more

MEDICINE, any substance, simple or compound, administered to a sick person for the cure or alleviation of disease.

The art of preventing, curing, or alleviating the diseases of the human body.

Figuratively, anything which serves to cure or correct a moral malady.

From the Latin medicina, from medeor, to heal, to cure.

Scripture uses it of a merry heart (Pro 17:22) and of the leaf of the tree by the sanctuary river (Eze 47:12).

Key Scripture

Pro 17:22 — "A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones."

Eze 47:12 — "And by the river upon the bank thereof, on this side and on that side, shall grow all trees for meat, whose leaf shall not fade, neither shall the fruit thereof be consumed: it shall bring forth new fruit according to his months, because their waters they issued out of the sanctuary: and the fruit thereof shall be for meat, and the leaf thereof for medicine."

Jer 30:13 — "There is none to plead thy cause, that thou mayest be bound up: thou hast no healing medicines."

Jer 46:11 — "Go up into Gilead, and take balm, O virgin, the daughter of Egypt: in vain shalt thou use many medicines; for thou shalt not be cured."

Modern Corruption

Two errors flank the doctrine of means: the sect that calls medicine unbelief, and the age that makes medicine its god; Scripture blesses the remedy and refuses it the throne.

expand to see more

On one side stand those who despise the means. Christian Science denies the reality of the disease outright; the harder wing of the Word-of-Faith movement treats a prescription as a confession of doubt, and children have died in that doctrine. Scripture gives it no quarter. Isaiah ordered a poultice of figs for a king whose recovery God had already sworn (2Ki 20:7). Paul told Timothy to leave off water and take a little wine for his stomach’s sake and his often infirmities (1Ti 5:23). Luke, the beloved physician, is named as such by the Holy Ghost without a word of apology (Col 4:14). And Christ Himself said that they that are whole need not a physician, but they that are sick (Luk 5:31) — an argument that assumes the physician’s office is good and useful, or the illustration collapses. To use the means God provides is not to distrust Him; it is to receive what He has given.

On the other side stands our own age, which has done to medicine what Judah did to Egypt: leaned on it as a saviour. Jeremiah’s taunt is exact — in vain shalt thou use many medicines, for thou shalt not be cured. When a civilisation can transplant an organ but cannot tell a man why he was made, it has multiplied remedies and lost the cure. Asa is the standing warning: in his disease he sought not to the LORD, but to the physicians, and the Chronicler records it as a fault, not for consulting them but for seeking to them instead of God. The Reformed doctrine of means walks between both ditches. God ordinarily works through second causes, so the believer takes the medicine, keeps the appointment, and thanks God for the physician; and God is never bound by the means, so the believer prays, submits, and knows that the leaf which finally heals the nations grows by a river that issues out of the sanctuary.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

A remedy applied to a wound — lawful, often effectual, never almighty.

expand to see more

Medicine — Latin medicina, from medeor, to heal.

Hebrew gehah, a cure; teruphah, a remedy or healing.

A merry heart works upon the body as a medicine works upon a sore (Pro 17:22).

The healing leaf grows by a river issuing out of the sanctuary (Eze 47:12).

Many medicines cannot cure a wound God has struck (Jer 46:11; Jer 30:13).

Usage

"A merry heart doeth good like a medicine — gladness in God is medicinal."

"Thou hast no healing medicines: the case that only God can take."

"Take the medicine and pray; the God who appoints the cure appoints the means."
